function.name: record_verdicts
function.description: Record the directional mastery verdicts for this pair, one judgment per direction.

verdict_a_to_b.description: Direction A to B. clear_yes = transfer is demonstrable: B's whole demand lives inside what mastering A requires, and the reason can point to where. likely = transfer is expected: no concrete fact, distinction or step of B's demand is missing from A, but the coverage rests on reading rather than demonstration. unlikely = transfer is doubtful: part of B's demand appears to sit outside mastering A, though no single decisive missing piece can be named. clear_no = transfer fails: the reason can name a fact, distinction or step B requires that mastering A does not carry. The middle levels record genuine uncertainty about this direction, not caution.

reason_a_to_b.description: One sentence on the A-to-B judgment. At the clear levels it points at the demonstration; at the middle levels, at the uncertainty.

verdict_b_to_a.description: Direction B to A, judged on its own merits with the roles reversed. clear_yes = transfer is demonstrable: A's whole demand lives inside what mastering B requires, and the reason can point to where. likely = transfer is expected: no concrete fact, distinction or step of A's demand is missing from B, but the coverage rests on reading rather than demonstration. unlikely = transfer is doubtful: part of A's demand appears to sit outside mastering B, though no single decisive missing piece can be named. clear_no = transfer fails: the reason can name a fact, distinction or step A requires that mastering B does not carry. The middle levels record genuine uncertainty about this direction, not caution.

reason_b_to_a.description: One sentence on the B-to-A judgment. At the clear levels it points at the demonstration; at the middle levels, at the uncertainty.

prompt.user_template:
You will read two knowledge items, A and B. Each is the knowledge behind
one assessment task and carries three fields: the knowledge statement, the
task that tests it, and the task's answer.

A piece of knowledge is identified not by its wording but by the pool of
fair test questions it lets a learner answer; in learning science this
unit is called a knowledge component. Between two components there can
hold a surmise relation: from observing that a learner masters one, one
may surmise that they also master the other — because whoever carries the
first's mastery thereby carries the second's. That surmise, and nothing
weaker, is the question.

You will judge it twice, once per direction, each on its own merits: the
two directions are separate questions, and matching or differing verdicts
are both ordinary outcomes.

First, A to B: take a learner who has genuinely mastered A — they
reliably answer fair questions of the kind A's task represents. May you
surmise, from that mastery alone, that they answer fair questions of the
kind B's task represents? The surmise holds only when B's whole demand
already lives inside A's; if B tests any fact, distinction or step that a
master of A may lack, the surmise fails, however close the two topics
are.

Then, B to A: the same question with the roles reversed — from genuine
mastery of B alone, may you surmise that the learner answers fair
questions of the kind A's task represents?

A surmise is an observed regularity, not a curriculum claim: it does not
say one item should be taught first, nor that one causes the other — only
that one's mastery carries the other's.

Use the record_verdicts tool once, carrying both judgments: for each
direction, choose the level that matches what you can actually show, with
a one-sentence reason.

<item_a>
<statement>{{a_statement}}</statement>
<task>{{a_task}}</task>
<answer>{{a_answer}}</answer>
</item_a>

<item_b>
<statement>{{b_statement}}</statement>
<task>{{b_task}}</task>
<answer>{{b_answer}}</answer>
</item_b>
